item.title: Interpreting a Photoelectron Spectrum of an Unknown Element
item.stimulus:
A student analyzes a gaseous sample of a single unknown element using photoelectron spectroscopy (PES). The photoelectron spectrum shows five peaks. The binding energy of each peak and its relative height (relative number of electrons) are listed in the table below.

Peak | Binding energy (MJ/mol) | Relative peak height
1 | 151 | 2
2 | 12.1 | 2
3 | 7.19 | 6
4 | 1.09 | 2
5 | 0.58 | 1

Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
item.model_answer:
(a) Peaks are assigned from highest to lowest binding energy: peak 1 = 1s, peak 2 = 2s, peak 3 = 2p, peak 4 = 3s, peak 5 = 3p. The relative peak heights are proportional to the number of electrons in each subshell, so the configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹. The total number of electrons is 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 13, so the element is aluminum (Al).

(b) Peak 1 corresponds to 1s electrons and peak 4 to 3s electrons. The 1s electrons are in the first shell, much closer to the nucleus, and are not shielded by any inner electrons, so they feel nearly the full +13 nuclear charge. The 3s electrons are in the third shell, farther from the nucleus, and are shielded by the 10 core electrons. By Coulomb's law, the 1s electrons are attracted much more strongly to the nucleus, so much more energy is needed to remove them.

(c) (i) The Si 1s peak will be at a binding energy greater than 151 MJ/mol. Si has 14 protons compared with 13 for Al. Its 1s electrons are in the same shell with essentially no shielding, so the larger nuclear charge attracts them more strongly, requiring more energy to remove them.
(ii) Si has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p², so the 3p peak has a relative height of 2 (twice the Al 3p peak).

(d) 0.58 MJ/mol × (10⁶ J / 1 MJ) = 5.8 × 10⁵ J/mol. (5.8 × 10⁵ J/mol) ÷ (6.022 × 10²³ electrons/mol) = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per electron.
item.verification_python:
import math
heights=[2,2,6,2,1]
assert sum(heights)==13
si=[2,2,6,2,2]
assert sum(si)==14 and si[4]==2
E=0.58e6/6.022e23
assert abs(E-9.63e-19)<0.01e-19
assert float('%.2g'%E)==9.6e-19
assert 151>1.09
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Identifying an Element from Photoelectron Spectrum Data
item.stimulus:
A gaseous sample of a single unknown element is analyzed by photoelectron spectroscopy (PES). High-energy photons eject electrons from every occupied subshell of the atoms. The binding energy of each peak and the relative height of each peak are listed below, from highest to lowest binding energy.

Peak | Binding energy (MJ/mol) | Relative peak height
1 | 208 | 2
2 | 18.7 | 2
3 | 13.5 | 6
4 | 1.95 | 2
5 | 1.06 | 3
item.model_answer:
(a) The relative peak heights give the number of electrons in each subshell: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons. A neutral atom with 15 electrons has atomic number 15, so the element is phosphorus. Assigning peaks in order of decreasing binding energy: peak 1 is 1s, peak 2 is 2s, peak 3 is 2p, peak 4 is 3s, peak 5 is 3p. The configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³.

(b) Peak 1 is from the 1s electrons and peak 4 is from the 3s electrons. The 1s electrons are in the first shell, much closer to the nucleus, and have no inner electrons shielding them, so they experience nearly the full nuclear charge. By Coulomb's law, the attraction is much stronger at smaller distance with greater effective nuclear charge, so much more energy is required to remove a 1s electron. The 3s electrons are farther from the nucleus and are shielded by the 10 electrons in the first and second shells, so they are held much less strongly.

(c) Greater than 208 MJ/mol. Sulfur has 16 protons compared with 15 for phosphorus. The 1s electrons in both atoms are in the same innermost shell, so the greater nuclear charge of sulfur attracts its 1s electrons more strongly, requiring more energy to remove them.

(d) Sulfur has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. The 3p subshell holds 4 electrons and the 3s subshell holds 2 electrons. Since peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in the subshell, the 3p peak is twice as tall as the 3s peak (4 : 2, or 2 : 1).
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction
heights_P = [2, 2, 6, 2, 3]
assert sum(heights_P) == 15
Z_P = 15
Z_S = 16
assert Z_S > Z_P
config_P = {'1s':2,'2s':2,'2p':6,'3s':2,'3p':3}
assert list(config_P.values()) == heights_P
config_S = {'1s':2,'2s':2,'2p':6,'3s':2,'3p':4}
assert sum(config_S.values()) == Z_S
assert Fraction(config_S['3p'], config_S['3s']) == Fraction(2,1)
be = [208, 18.7, 13.5, 1.95, 1.06]
assert all(be[i] > be[i+1] for i in range(len(be)-1))
inner = config_P['1s'] + config_P['2s'] + config_P['2p']
assert inner == 10
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Identify the unknown element and write its complete ground-state electron configuration. Justify the identity using the PES data.

criteria.text: Identifies the element as phosphorus (P) by summing the relative peak heights to 15 electrons, equal to the atomic number of a neutral atom.
criteria.evidence: States phosphorus and shows or states that the peak heights total 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons, so Z = 15.
criteria.fix: Add all relative peak heights to find the total electrons; for a neutral atom this equals the atomic number, then locate it on the periodic table.

criteria.text: Writes the ground-state configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, matching each peak to a subshell.
criteria.evidence: Gives 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, consistent with the peak heights in order of decreasing binding energy.
criteria.fix: Assign peaks in order of decreasing binding energy to 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, using each peak height as the electron count.

parts.prompt: The binding energy of peak 1 (208 MJ/mol) is much greater than that of peak 4 (1.95 MJ/mol). Explain this difference in terms of the interactions between the electrons and the nucleus.

criteria.text: Explains that 1s electrons (peak 1) are much closer to the nucleus and experience little shielding, so they feel a stronger Coulombic attraction than 3s electrons (peak 4).
criteria.evidence: Identifies peak 1 as 1s and peak 4 as 3s, and attributes the higher binding energy to smaller distance from the nucleus and/or less shielding, giving stronger Coulombic attraction.
criteria.fix: Link binding energy to Coulomb's law: name the subshells, then compare distance from the nucleus and shielding by inner electrons.

parts.prompt: Predict whether the 1s peak in the PES spectrum of sulfur would appear at a binding energy greater than, less than, or equal to 208 MJ/mol. Justify your prediction.

criteria.text: Predicts the sulfur 1s peak is at a binding energy greater than 208 MJ/mol because sulfur has one more proton (16 vs 15), increasing the nuclear attraction on 1s electrons at a similar distance.
criteria.evidence: Claims greater than 208 MJ/mol and justifies with the larger nuclear charge of sulfur attracting the 1s electrons more strongly.
criteria.fix: Compare the number of protons in the two nuclei; electrons in the same innermost subshell are held more tightly by a larger nuclear charge.

parts.prompt: In the PES spectrum of sulfur, the lowest-energy peak corresponds to the 3p subshell. State the relative height of this 3p peak compared with the 3s peak of sulfur, and justify your answer using the electron configuration of sulfur.

criteria.text: States the sulfur 3p peak is twice as tall as its 3s peak (ratio 4 : 2) because sulfur's configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.
criteria.evidence: Gives a 2 : 1 ratio (or 4 : 2) and supports it with 3p⁴ and 3s² from the sulfur electron configuration, linking peak height to electron number.
criteria.fix: Write the configuration first, then remember peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.

item.title: Interpreting the Photoelectron Spectrum of an Unknown Element
item.stimulus:
A student obtains the photoelectron spectrum of a gaseous sample of an unknown element X. All atoms are in the ground state. The spectrum shows five peaks. The binding energy of each peak and its relative peak height are listed below.

Peak | Binding energy (MJ/mol) | Relative peak height
1 | 210 | 2
2 | 18.7 | 2
3 | 13.5 | 6
4 | 1.95 | 2
5 | 1.06 | 3

Answer the following.
item.model_answer:
(a) In PES, the relative height of each peak is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell. Assigning subshells from highest to lowest binding energy: peak 1 = 1s (2 electrons), peak 2 = 2s (2), peak 3 = 2p (6), peak 4 = 3s (2), peak 5 = 3p (3). The configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. The total is 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons, so a neutral atom has 15 protons and X is phosphorus.

(b) Peak 1 corresponds to 1s electrons and peak 4 to 3s electrons. The 1s electrons are in the first shell, much closer to the nucleus, and have no inner electrons shielding them, so they experience a much greater effective nuclear charge. By Coulomb's law, the attraction between the nucleus and the 1s electrons is much stronger than for the 3s electrons, which are farther away and shielded by the 10 electrons in the first and second shells. Therefore much more energy is required to remove a 1s electron.

(c) Sulfur has 16 electrons, with configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. The peak with the lowest binding energy corresponds to the 3p subshell, which holds 4 electrons, so its relative height is 4.

(d) The sulfur 1s peak appears at a binding energy greater than 210 MJ/mol. Sulfur has 16 protons compared with 15 for phosphorus, while its 1s electrons are still in the first shell at a similar distance and with no shielding. The greater nuclear charge attracts the 1s electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove them.
item.verification_python:
heights={'1s':2,'2s':2,'2p':6,'3s':2,'3p':3}
total=sum(heights.values())
assert total==15
Z_P=15
assert total==Z_P
energies=[210,18.7,13.5,1.95,1.06]
assert energies==sorted(energies,reverse=True)
assert energies[0]>energies[3]
# sulfur configuration
Z_S=16
caps=[('1s',2),('2s',2),('2p',6),('3s',2),('3p',6)]
rem=Z_S
conf={}
for s,c in caps:
    n=min(c,rem)
    conf[s]=n
    rem-=n
assert conf=={'1s':2,'2s':2,'2p':6,'3s':2,'3p':4}
assert conf['3p']==4
assert Z_S>Z_P
inner=heights['1s']+heights['2s']+heights['2p']
assert inner==10
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
